passages.t: Called up, to worship at a distance
passages.happening: “Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Come up to the LORD’” (verse 1). Aaron, his sons Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders are to come too, “and you are to worship at a distance” (verse 1). “Moses alone shall approach the LORD, but the others must not come near. And the people may not go up with him” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 19 offered the covenant. Chapters 20 to 23 set out its terms. Chapter 24 seals it. This is the formal making of the covenant at Sinai, the bond on which the rest of the Old Testament's story depends. When the prophets later accuse Israel of breaking the covenant, this is the day they have in mind.

The chapter opens with a careful order of who may come how close. The people stay at the foot of the mountain. Aaron, his two eldest sons Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders go partway and worship ‘at a distance’. Moses alone goes near.

That order will be built into the tabernacle in the chapters that follow: an outer courtyard, a holy place, and an inner room where only one man may go. God is coming close to his people. He is also holy, and coming near him is not a small thing.

Nadab and Abihu are among the few called up here. Later they died for offering fire God had not commanded. Being near God on a great day did not guarantee faithfulness afterward.
passages.later:
Leviticus tells what became of Aaron's sons: they “offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command” (Leviticus 10:1).

Hebrews sets this mountain beside another. Believers have not come to a mountain they cannot touch, but “to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).
passages.asks: Some came near and some stayed at a distance, and all were called to worship. Ask how near you think you may come to God, and on what ground. And ask whether closeness to holy things has ever made you careless with them.

passages.t: ‘This is the blood of the covenant’
passages.happening:
Moses tells the people all the LORD's words, “they all responded with one voice: ‘All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do’” (verse 3).

“And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD” (verse 4). Early next morning he builds an altar at the foot of the mountain, “along with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel” (verse 4). Young men offer burnt offerings and peace offerings (verse 5). Moses puts half the blood in bowls and sprinkles half on the altar (verse 6).

“Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it to the people, who replied, ‘All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient’” (verse 7).

“So Moses took the blood, sprinkled it on the people, and said, ‘This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words’” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world agreements were sealed with ritual: the terms written down, read aloud before witnesses, an oath, a sacrifice, and often a shared meal. This covenant has every one. The words are written. Twelve standing stones stand for the twelve tribes. The scroll is read. The people swear. The blood is applied. In the next scene the leaders eat.

The people answer twice. The second time they add ‘we will be obedient’. In Hebrew it is, word for word, that they will hear.

Then the blood. In Israel blood meant life, and above all life given up in death. Half goes on the altar, which stands for God. Half goes on the people. Both sides are bound in one bond of life and death. Some readers compare the older covenant of Genesis 15, where animals were cut in two and the one who passed between them called death on himself if he broke faith. Others stress the cleansing power of blood, so that the people are both bound to God and made fit to belong to him.

‘This is the blood of the covenant.’ Jesus takes up those words at his last supper.

The promise is sincere, and it is short-lived. Within weeks these same people will make a golden calf (chapter 32).
passages.later:
At his last supper Jesus took the cup and said, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24). Luke gives it as “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20), the new covenant Jeremiah promised (Jeremiah 31:31).

Hebrews quotes this scene: “That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood” (Hebrews 9:18), and “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep” (Hebrews 9:20).

Leviticus gives the reason blood mattered: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11).

The reading of the scroll was to go on. Deuteronomy commands that every seventh year “you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel” (Deuteronomy 31:11).
passages.asks: The people said twice, with one voice, that they would do all God said. Ask what you have promised God, and whether you said it more easily than you have kept it. And ask what it means that the covenant rests in the end on blood given for you, not on the strength of your promise.

passages.t: They saw God, and ate and drank
passages.happening:
“Then Moses went up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and they saw the God of Israel” (verses 9-10). “Under His feet was a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself” (verse 10).

“But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
These are some of the most startling words in the Old Testament. The leaders of Israel ‘saw the God of Israel’.

Notice what the text describes. Nothing of God's form. Only what lies under his feet: a pavement like sapphire, clear as the sky. The stone is probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone prized in Egypt and Mesopotamia and linked with the heavens.

Notice, too, the surprise: ‘God did not lay His hand on’ them. They were not struck down.

Then they ate and drank. A shared meal was the ordinary way to seal an agreement in that world, as when Jacob and Laban ate together on a mountain after their covenant. Here the meal is eaten in the presence of the King himself, probably from the meat of the peace offerings. The covenant ends not in fear but at a table.
passages.later:
Jacob and Laban sealed their covenant the same way: “Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat a meal” (Genesis 31:54).

Isaiah looks ahead to another meal on a mountain: “On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples” (Isaiah 25:6). Revelation speaks of ‘the marriage supper of the Lamb’ (Revelation 19:9).
passages.hard:
The elders saw the God of Israel. Doesn't the Bible say no one can see God and live?

It does. God tells Moses, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (33:20), and John writes, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

The text itself feels the tension. It describes nothing of God's form, only the pavement under his feet, and it notes with surprise that God did not strike them. Interpreters handle this in several ways. Many make a distinction between seeing God in a vision or a showing of his glory, and seeing his unveiled face, which no creature could survive. Christian readers have often added that such appearances in the Old Testament were God made known through the Son, who, in John's words, ‘has made Him known’. Ancient translators felt the difficulty too. The Greek translation says they saw the place where the God of Israel stood.

Every reading agrees that what the elders saw was real and also partial: a gift of grace that let them live.
passages.asks: The covenant was sealed with a meal in God's presence. Ask whether you think of God as one you could sit at a table with. And ask what the Lord's Supper means to you when you hear that this meal came first.

passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Come up to Me on the mountain and stay here, so that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction’” (verse 12).

Moses goes up with Joshua his attendant (verse 13), and tells the elders to wait, with Aaron and Hur to settle disputes (verse 14).

“When Moses went up on the mountain, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai. For six days the cloud covered it, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud” (verses 15-16).

“And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites” (verse 17). Moses entered the cloud “and he remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Moses goes up to receive the tablets. While he is there, God gives him the plans for the tabernacle, which fill chapters 25 to 31.

Joshua, who led the battle against Amalek, goes with him as his helper. Hur, who held up Moses' hands in that battle (17:12), stays with Aaron to keep order below.

‘Glory’ is kavod, from a root meaning heavy or weighty. Used of God, it names the visible splendor of his presence. To the people below it looked like fire on the mountaintop.

‘Settled’ is shakan, to dwell. The Hebrew name for the tabernacle, mishkan, dwelling place, comes from the same verb. Later Jewish writers used a related word, Shekinah, for God's dwelling presence.

Six days of waiting and a call on the seventh echo the week of creation. And the glory that rests on the mountain here will fill the finished tabernacle in the book's last scene (40:34). The presence on the mountain is about to go with Israel on the road.
passages.later:
Jesus fasted “forty days and forty nights” in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2), a link of theme rather than a stated fulfillment.

Hebrews says of God, in words drawn from Sinai, that he is ‘a consuming fire’ (Hebrews 12:29).
passages.asks: Moses waited six days before God spoke. Ask whether you are willing to wait in God's presence when nothing seems to happen. And ask what it means that the God of consuming fire chose to come and live among his people.
